newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's dollar ends weaker in light trading.
newsitem.headline: Canada's dollar ends weaker in light trading.

text.p: FORECAST RANGE 1.3840/1.3880 ASIAN CLOSE 1.3858
RESISTANCE 1.3795 SUPPORT 1.3945 HI 1.3877 LO 1.3860
CANADA OPEN 1.3862/67 HI 1.3877 EUROPE OPEN 1.3825

* Canada's dollar closed slightly weaker at C$1.3868 (US$0.7210) in light trading on Wednesday despite Prime Minister Jean Chretien's announcement that Paul Martin would remain finance minister in the new cabinet, traders said. * They said the unit was stuck in a narrow range of C$1.3840 (US$0.7225) and C$1.3880 (US$0.7204) for the entire session.
There had been rumors in the markets since last week's federal election that the deficit-slashing Martin might be moved out of finance and into a national unity portfolio.
But Martin's confirmation failed to give even a slight boost to the Canadian currency.
"That was pretty well a done deal for a long time, so it's not surprising that nothing happened," one trader said.
The continuing surge of the Japanese yen also hurt the tone of the Canada dollar, which dropped to 80.16 yen in late afternoon trading from Tuesday's 80.96 yen.
U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers triggered the yen strength on Wednesday when he said that Japan should avoid running up external surpluses that would hurt global growth.
Summers was reacting to a report showing Japan's trade surplus and current account continued to grow at a healthy clip in April.

But the Canada dollar fared better than the U.S. dollar, which continued its one-month collapse against the yen. The U.S. dollar touched 111.55 yen in Tokyo trading on Wednesday, down 13 percent from a peak of 127.47 on May 1.
"Today, we are seeing good two-way business in Canada-yen trade," said William Chin, vice-president of foreign exchange with ABN-AMRO Bank.
"Another way of putting it is that the Canada dollar is doing better in the face of the ever-improving yen," Chin added.

Analysts said the Canadian dollar would probably not break out of its narrow trading range until it became clear whether U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan planned to raise short-term interest rates at the next FOMC meeting scheduled for July 1-2.

"It is not going to be a clear-cut case of what the Fed will do in July, so the (Canada) dollar is going to remain range-bound until we hit that date," said John Anania, economist with Royal Bank of Canada.
Anania said that any hesitation by the Bank of Canada to match a July Fed hike would cause turbulence for the Canadian dollar.
"We see some possible weakness coming out of there because we don't think the (central) bank is going to move right away to match the hike," Anania said.
On the crosses, the Canadian dollar dipped to 1.2367 marks from Tuesday's 1.2372 marks.
((Paul Simao, Reuters Toronto Bureau (416) 941-8104))
